claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: When more CaM was added to 15N-labeled H1 (at 3:1 CaM:H1 ratio), the set of signals originating from H1 bound to the N-lobe decreased in intensity and vanished, with the peptide almost exclusively bound to the higher affinity C-lobe of CaM.
claims.source: When more CaM was added, the set of signals originating from H1 bound to the N-lobe decreased in intensity and vanished at a molar ratio of 3:1 (CaM:H1). At this condition, the peptide was almost exclusively bound to the higher affinity C-lobe of CaM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: Titration of H2 into 15N-labeled CaM showed NMR signals gradually moving with increasing peptide concentration, indicating the free and bound states to be in fast exchange on the NMR timescale.
claims.source: We next titrated 15N-labeled CaM with the low-affinity H2 peptide. Here, in contrast to the H1 titration, the NMR signals were gradually moving with increasing peptide concentration, indicating the free and bound states to be in fast exchange on the NMR timescale (kex > Δδ, Figure 2e–f, Prestel et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2e–f and citation to NMR methodology.

claims.claim: 2D NMR lineshape analysis of H2:CaM interaction resulted in affinity and dissociation rate constants of Kd = 16 ± 1 µM and koff = 2600 ± 100 s−1, respectively.
claims.source: The change in peak position could be followed throughout the titration, and 2D NMR lineshape analysis resulted in affinity and dissociation rate constants of Kd = 16 ± 1 µM and koff = 2600 ± 100 s−1, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR lineshape analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and Table 2.

claims.claim: Chemical shift perturbations induced by H2 binding spanned both CaM lobes, although they were less pronounced for the C-lobe and generally smaller compared to those induced by H1 binding.
claims.source: Again, the CSPs spanned both CaM lobes (Figure 2h), although they were less pronounced for the C-lobe and generally smaller compared to those induced by H1 binding.
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 2h.

claims.claim: Each of the CaM lobes can bind one NHE1 H1 with high affinity forming a 1:2 complex, with the C-lobe energetically slightly favored.
claims.source: Taken together, these data show that each of the CaM lobes can bind one NHE1 H1 with high affinity forming a 1:2 complex, with the C-lobe energetically slightly favored.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMR and ITC data.

claims.claim: CaM binds NHE1 H2 with lower affinity in a 1:1 complex with both CaM lobes involved.
claims.source: CaM binds NHE1 H2 with lower affinity in a 1:1 complex with both CaM lobes involved, suggesting a more classical CaM binding as depicted in the cartoon in Figure 2g.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMR and ITC data, depicted in Figure 2g.

claims.claim: At a molar ratio of 1:2 (CaM:H1H2), the 15N HSQC spectrum closely resembled the state where only H1 is present in twofold excess.
claims.source: At a molar ratio of 1:2 (CaM:H1H2), the 15N HSQC spectrum closely resembled the state where only H1 is present in twofold excess (Figure 3a–c).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3a–c.

claims.claim: At 1:2 stoichiometry (CaM:H1H2), each CaM lobe interacts with one H1 of H1H2 in a ternary complex, while H2 is not involved in the interaction.
claims.source: This suggested that at this stoichiometry each CaM lobe interacts with one H1 of H1H2 in a ternary complex, while H2 is not involved in the interaction, as depicted in Figure 3a.
claims.evidence: Inferred from NMR data and depicted in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: At a stoichiometry of 1:1 (CaM:H1H2), the signals of the N-lobe of CaM overlaid with the spectrum of CaM at saturation with H1, while signals of the C-lobe overlaid with the spectrum of CaM bound to H2.
claims.source: At a stoichiometry of 1:1, the signals of the N-lobe of CaM still overlaid almost perfectly with the spectrum of 15N-labeled CaM at saturation with H1. However, signals of the C-lobe now overlaid with the spectrum of CaM bound to H2 (Figure 3d–f).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3d–f.

claims.claim: At 1:1 molar ratio (CaM:H1H2), the major state is the N-lobe of CaM bound to H1 and the C-lobe bound to H2.
claims.source: Thus, at this molar ratio, the major state is the N-lobe of CaM bound to H1 and the C-lobe bound to H2, as depicted in Figure 3d.
claims.evidence: Inferred from NMR data and depicted in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: A second set of very weak NMR peaks was detectable for many residues at 1:1 (CaM:H1H2) stoichiometry, suggesting the presence of a minor state with the opposite architecture: the N-lobe of CaM bound to H2 and the C-lobe bound to H1.
claims.source: It is worth noting that a second set of very weak peaks was detectable for many of the residues. Comparing these to the spectra from the simpler systems of the individual peptides, this suggested the presence of a minor state with the opposite architecture: the N-lobe of CaM bound to H2 and the C-lobe bound to H1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The severely broadened NMR signals at 1:1 (CaM:H1H2) stoichiometry may be explained by exchange between two states, with the equilibrium highly shifted toward the H1:N-lobe;H2:C-lobe complex.
claims.source: The severely broadened signals may thus be explained by exchange between these two states, and judging from the relative signal intensities, the equilibrium was highly shifted toward the H1:N-lobe;H2:C-lobe complex, as depicted in Figure 3d.
claims.evidence: Inferred from NMR data and depicted in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: At a stoichiometry of 1:2 (CaM:H1H2), two sets of signals originated from each residue of H1 in 15N-labeled H1H2, while signals from H2 closely resembled those of unbound H2.
claims.source: At a stoichiometry of 1:2 (CaM:H1H2), two sets of signals originated from each residue of H1, while signals from H2 closely resembled those of unbound H2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claims.claim: At a stoichiometry of 1:1 (CaM:H1H2), signals from H1 in 15N-labeled H1H2 overlapped with the N-lobe bound state, while signals from H2 were either invisible or closely resembled the C-lobe bound state.
claims.source: At a stoichiometry of 1:1, signals from H1 overlapped with the N-lobe bound state, while signals from H2 were either invisible or closely resembled the C-lobe bound state (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2d.

claims.claim: At 1:1 and 1:2 (CaM:H1H2) stoichiometries, the NMR signals were drastically broadened compared to those of free CaM or of the 1:2 complex saturated with H1, indicating a dynamic equilibrium of states with different stoichiometries.
claims.source: It is, however, important to note that at 1:1 as well as 1:2 (CaM:H1H2) stoichiometries the NMR signals were drastically broadened compared to those of free CaM or of the 1:2 complex saturated with H1 (Figure 3a, d), indicating a dynamic equilibrium of states with different stoichiometries, including potential higher order oligomers.
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3a, d.

claims.claim: The mass of the CaM:H1H2 complex at a 1:1 stoichiometry as determined from SEC-MALS (25.0 ± 1.6 kDa) was in perfect agreement with the expected molecular weight of a 1:1 complex (25.5 kDa).
claims.source: The mass of the complex at a 1:1 stoichiometry as determined from SEC-MALS (25.0 ± 1.6 kDa) was in perfect agreement with the expected molecular weight of a 1:1 complex (25.5 kDa) and suggested that, if higher oligomers were present, their population was low under these conditions.
claims.evidence: Supported by SEC-MALS data.

claims.claim: DLS and PFG-NMR showed a stepwise increase of the complex size from free CaM to the complexes formed at 1:1 and 1:2 stoichiometries, respectively.
claims.source: However, these complexes were readily accessible by DLS and PFG-NMR: both experiment series showed a stepwise increase of the complex size from free CaM to the complexes formed at 1:1 and 1:2 stoichiometries, respectively.
claims.evidence: Supported by DLS and PFG-NMR data.

claims.claim: The NMR solution structure of the ternary complex shows that both CaM lobes have one H1 bound inside the hydrophobic cleft.
claims.source: Both CaM lobes have one H1 bound inside the hydrophobic cleft (Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR structure shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: An overlay of the 10 lowest energy structures shows that the individual lobes are well defined (backbone RMSD: N-lobe + H1N = 0.77 ± 0.16 Å; backbone RMSD C-lobe + H1c = 0.83 ± 0.18 Å), while no NOEs between the two lobes could be obtained, suggesting that the linker region remains flexible in the bound state.
claims.source: An overlay of the 10 lowest energy structures shows that the individual lobes are well defined (backbone RMSD: N-lobe + H1N = 0.77 ± 0.16 Å; backbone RMSD C-lobe + H1c = 0.83 ± 0.18 Å), while no NOEs between the two lobes could be obtained, suggesting that the linker region remains flexible in the bound state (Figure 4b, c).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR structure data shown in Figure 4b, c.

claims.claim: In both lobes, the interaction surface is defined by contacts between the hydrophobic face of the amphipathic H1 (L623, I631, I634, L635, N638, L639, T642, and L646) and the central methionines in the hydrophobic cleft of each CaM-lobe.
claims.source: In both lobes, the interaction surface is defined by contacts between the hydrophobic face of the amphipathic H1 (L623, I631, I634, L635, N638, L639, T642, and L646; Figure 4d, e) and the central methionines in the hydrophobic cleft of each CaM-lobe.
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR structure data shown in Figure 4d, e.

claims.claim: For the N-lobe, the interaction involves M37, M52, M72, and M73; and for the C-lobe M110, M125, M145, and M146.
claims.source: For the N-lobe, this involves M37, M52, M72, and M73; and for the C-lobe M110, M125, M145, and M146.
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR structure data.

claims.claim: A high complementarity in electrostatics is evident, with multiple positively charged residues on the opposite side of NHE1 H1 (K625, K637, R632, K633, R636, K641, R643, R645) complementing the negatively charged surface of CaM.
claims.source: In addition, a high complementarity in electrostatics is evident, with multiple positively charged residues on the opposite side of NHE1 H1 (K625, K637, R632, K633, R636, K641, R643, R645) complementing the negatively charged surface of CaM (Figure 4f–i).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR structure data shown in Figure 4f–i.

claims.claim: The mode of interaction between the CaM C-lobe and H1 described by NMR was also present in the crystal structure, but was translated as crystal contacts between symmetry-related molecules.
claims.source: Although this complex is very different from that shown in the published crystal structure (Köster et al., 2011), inspection of the neighboring molecules in the crystal lattice reveals that the mode of interaction between the CaM C-lobe and H1, which we describe here by NMR, was also present in the crystal, but was translated as crystal contacts between symmetry-related molecules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of NMR structure with crystal structure shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the absence of Ca2+, chemical shift perturbations and line broadening of apo-CaM were observable after addition of excess NHE1 H1H2, showing that NHE1:CaM complex formation can also occur in the absence of Ca2+.
claims.source: In the absence of Ca2+, we still observed CSPs of CaM after addition of 2.5-fold molar excess of H1H2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a), suggesting that also the Ca2+-free form of CaM binds NHE1 H1H2.
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: Under conditions where both Ca2+ and high EDTA were present, in the additional presence of 2.5-fold molar excess of H1H2, signals of the C-lobe overlapped with those from Ca2+-CaM bound to H1, while signals of the N-lobe closely resembled the Ca2+-free state.
claims.source: Under conditions where both Ca2+ (here 2 mM) and high EDTA (here 6.6 mM) were present, free CaM gets stripped of Ca2+. However, in the additional presence of 2.5-fold molar excess of H1H2, signals of the C-lobe overlapped with those from Ca2+-CaM bound to H1, while signals of the N-lobe closely resembled the Ca2+-free state (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claims.claim: The presence of H1 increased the affinity for Ca2+ in the C-lobe of CaM.
claims.source: Thus, the presence of H1 increased the affinity for Ca2+ in the C-lobe.
claims.evidence: Inferred from NMR data showing Ca2+ binding to C-lobe in presence of H1 under Ca2+-limiting conditions.

claims.claim: S648 is located at the C-terminal distal end of H1.
claims.source: S648, which can be phosphorylated by Akt (Meima et al., 2009; Snabaitis et al., 2008), is located at the C-terminal distal end of H1.
claims.evidence: Describes the location of S648 based on sequence and structural information.

claims.claim: In cardiomyocytes, the S648A mutation increased CaM binding to NHE1 in vitro, and S648 phosphorylation by Akt was proposed to inhibit NHE1 by preventing CaM binding.
claims.source: In cardiomyocytes, the S648A mutation increased CaM binding to NHE1 in vitro, and S648 phosphorylation by Akt was proposed to inhibit NHE1 by preventing CaM binding (Snabaitis et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior study in cardiomyocytes.

claims.claim: In fibroblasts, S648 phosphorylation by Akt was required for NHE1 activation by platelet-derived growth factor.
claims.source: In contrast, in fibroblasts, S648 phosphorylation by Akt was required for NHE1 activation by platelet-derived growth factor (Meima et al., 2009), indicating that the impact of this residue may be cell-type- and/or context-specific.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior study in fibroblasts.

claims.claim: WT NHE1 and all three variants (H1-CR, S648A, S648D) localized primarily to the plasma membrane in PS120 cells.
claims.source: WT NHE1 and all three variants localized primarily to the plasma membrane – the expected pattern for exogenously expressed NHE1 localization in PS120 cells (Figure 5; Denker and Barber, 2002; Hendus-Altenburger et al., 2016; Hendus-Altenburger et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5 and citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: NHE1 protein expression levels were comparable between cell lines, albeit slightly higher in cells expressing the variants compared to WT.
claims.source: NHE1 protein expression levels were comparable between cell lines, albeit slightly higher in cells expressing the variants compared to WT, as shown by immunoblot analysis (Figure 5b, c).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5b, c.

claims.claim: Endogenous CaM exhibited similar expression levels in all cell lines.
claims.source: As expected, endogenous CaM exhibited similar expression levels in all cell lines (Figure 5b, d) and localized mainly diffusely in the cytosol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5b, d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The steady-state pHi was similar between all cell lines, ranging from ~7.4 to 7.5.
claims.source: The steady-state pHi was similar between all cell lines, ranging from ~7.4 to 7.5 (Figure 5e).
claims.evidence: Supported by pHi measurement data shown in Figure 5e.

claims.claim: Following an acid load without further stimulation, recovery rates were not significantly different between cells expressing WT and variant NHE1s.
claims.source: Following an acid load without further stimulation, recovery rates were not significantly different between cells expressing WT and variant NHE1s (Figure 5f, g).
claims.evidence: Supported by pHi recovery data shown in Figure 5f, g.

claims.claim: In the presence of ionomycin, cells expressing WT NHE1 recovered significantly faster than WT vehicle controls.
claims.source: In the presence of the Ca2+-ionophore ionomycin, which causes elevated [Ca2+]i, added concomitantly with the acid load, cells expressing WT NHE1 recovered significantly faster than WT vehicle controls (Figure 5h, i), in agreement with previous reports (Wakabayashi et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: Supported by pHi recovery data shown in Figure 5h, i and citation to prior study.

claims.claim: Under ionomycin-stimulated conditions, recovery was significantly reduced in cells expressing the NHE1 H1-CR and S648D variants compared to those expressing WT NHE1.
claims.source: Under ionomycin-stimulated conditions, recovery was significantly reduced in cells expressing the NHE1 H1-CR and S648D variants compared to those expressing WT NHE1 (Figure 5h, i).
claims.evidence: Supported by pHi recovery data shown in Figure 5h, i.

claims.claim: PLA puncta representing ≤40 nM proximity of CaM and NHE1 were clearly detected in PS120 cells expressing WT NHE1.
claims.source: In PS120 cells expressing WT NHE1, PLA puncta, representing ≤40 nM proximity of CaM and NHE1, were clearly detected (Figure 6a, b).
claims.evidence: Supported by PLA data shown in Figure 6a, b.

claims.claim: The number of PLA puncta per area did not increase upon ionomycin treatment.
claims.source: The number of PLA puncta per area did not increase upon ionomycin treatment (Figure 6a, b), suggesting that an increase in [Ca2+]i does not detectably increase the number of CaM and NHE1 proteins within close proximity of each other.
claims.evidence: Supported by PLA data shown in Figure 6a, b.

claims.claim: None of the three variants (H1-CR, S648A, S648D) abolished NHE1:CaM PLA in situ.
claims.source: In contrast to their inhibitory effect on Ca2+-induced NHE1 activation (Figure 5h, i), none of the three variants abolished NHE1:CaM PLA in situ (Figure 6a, b).
claims.evidence: Supported by PLA data shown in Figure 6a, b.

claims.claim: In the NMR solution structure of the 1:2 (CaM:H1) complex, the four residues K641, R643, R645, and R648 are all solvent exposed both when bound to the N-lobe or the C-lobe of CaM.
claims.source: In the complex, the four residues K641, R643, R645, and R648 are all solvent exposed both when bound to the N-lobe or the C-lobe of CaM, with some hydrophobic contacts from K641 (Figure 6c, d).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR structure data shown in Figure 6c, d.

claims.claim: In either of the lobes, S648 does not form direct contacts with CaM.
claims.source: Likewise, in either of the lobes, S648 does not form direct contacts with CaM (Figure 6c, d).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR structure data shown in Figure 6c, d.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of a single residue by Akt was confirmed by mass spectrometry, and S648 was identified by NMR.
claims.source: Phosphorylation of a single residue by Akt was confirmed by mass spectrometry, and S648 was identified by NMR, while PKCδ gave rise to mono-, double-, and triple phosphorylated forms of H1H2, identified by NMR at residues T642, S648, and T653 (Figure 6h, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry and NMR data shown in Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: PKCδ gave rise to mono-, double-, and triple phosphorylated forms of H1H2, identified by NMR at residues T642, S648, and T653.
claims.source: Phosphorylation of a single residue by Akt was confirmed by mass spectrometry, and S648 was identified by NMR, while PKCδ gave rise to mono-, double-, and triple phosphorylated forms of H1H2, identified by NMR at residues T642, S648, and T653 (Figure 6h, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry and NMR data shown in Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of S648 results in a tenfold weakened binding to CaM compared to WT (Kd,1 = 5 ± 4 nM for first binding event, Kd,2 = 2700 ± 600 nM for second binding event).
claims.source: The first binding event gave a Kd,1 = 5 ± 4 nM with a stoichiometry n1 = 0.93 ± 0.02, while the second binding event gave a Kd,1 = 2700 ± 600 nM with n2 = 1.16 ± 0.06 (Figure 6i, Table 1). Thus, indeed, phosphorylation of S648 results in a tenfold weakened binding to CaM compared to WT.
claims.evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 6i and Table 1.

claims.claim: A 10 min stimulation with ionomycin had no detectable effect on Akt activation (phosphorylation) in PS120 cells.
claims.source: A 10 min stimulation with ionomycin had no detectable effect on Akt activation (phosphorylation) in PS120 cells (Figure 6g).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6g.

claims.claim: Akt activity was ablated under both control and ionomycin conditions by the Akt inhibitor Akti-1/2.
claims.source: Furthermore, Akt activity was ablated under both control and ionomycin conditions by the Akt inhibitor Akti-1/2 (Figure 6g), yet Akti-1/2 had no significant effect on ionomycin-stimulated NHE1 activity after an acid load (Figure 6e).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot and pHi recovery data shown in Figure 6g and Figure 6e.

claims.claim: Akti-1/2 had no significant effect on ionomycin-stimulated NHE1 activity after an acid load.
claims.source: Furthermore, Akt activity was ablated under both control and ionomycin conditions by the Akt inhibitor Akti-1/2 (Figure 6g), yet Akti-1/2 had no significant effect on ionomycin-stimulated NHE1 activity after an acid load (Figure 6e).
claims.evidence: Supported by pHi recovery data shown in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: Two PKC inhibitors, bisindolylmaleimide I (BIM I) and Gö6983, had no significant effects on the Ca2+-dependent NHE1 activity after acidification.
claims.source: Similarly, two well-established PKC inhibitors, bisindolylmaleimide I (BIM I) – targeting PKCα, -β1, -β2, -γ, -δ, and -ε – and Gö6983 – targeting PKCα, PKCβ, -γ, -δ, and -ζ (Figure 6f) – also had no significant effects on the Ca2+-dependent NHE1 activity after acidification.
claims.evidence: Supported by pHi recovery data shown in Figure 6f.

claims.claim: In solution, NHE1 and CaM can form either 1:1 or 2:1 (NHE1:CaM) complexes with similar affinities but different structures.
claims.source: In vitro, we found that NHE1 and CaM can form either 1:1 or 2:1 (NHE1:CaM) complexes with similar affinities but different structures, suggesting that the complex is highly dynamic and that the relevant state at any time is dependent on the availability of Ca2+-CaM and NHE1 in the cell (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMR and ITC data, depicted in Figure 7.

claims.claim: In the absence of Ca2+, apo-CaM can associate weakly with NHE1-binding sites in a different type of complex.
claims.source: In the absence of Ca2+, apo-CaM can associate weakly with NHE1-binding sites in a different type of complex (Figure 7c).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data and depicted in Figure 7c.

claims.claim: At low Ca2+ levels, NHE1:CaM interaction can stabilize Ca2+-binding to the C-lobe of CaM, resulting in an apo-state N-lobe and a Ca2+-loaded C-lobe bound to H1.
claims.source: Under such low Ca2+ conditions, our results show that in vitro NHE1:CaM interaction can stabilize Ca2+-binding to the C-lobe of CaM, resulting in an apo-state N-lobe and a Ca2+-loaded C-lobe bound to H1 (Figure 7d).
claims.evidence: Supported by NMR data and depicted in Figure 7d.

claims.claim: At higher [Ca2+-CaM], two scenarios are possible: one is a 1:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the major state having the N-lobe bound to H1 and the C-lobe bound to H2.
claims.source: At higher [Ca2+-CaM], corresponding to, for example, mitogenic stimuli, which can increase [Ca2+]i to up to around 1 µM, the present study indicates that two scenarios are possible: one is a 1:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the major state having the N-lobe bound to H1 and the C-lobe bound to H2 (Figure 7e), and the second is a 2:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the CaM N- and C-lobes both interacting with H1 on two adjacent NHE1 C-tails, potentially stabilizing the dimeric state of NHE1 (Figure 7f).
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMR data and depicted in Figure 7e.

claims.claim: At higher [Ca2+-CaM], the second scenario is a 2:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the CaM N- and C-lobes both interacting with H1 on two adjacent NHE1 C-tails, potentially stabilizing the dimeric state of NHE1.
claims.source: At higher [Ca2+-CaM], corresponding to, for example, mitogenic stimuli, which can increase [Ca2+]i to up to around 1 µM, the present study indicates that two scenarios are possible: one is a 1:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the major state having the N-lobe bound to H1 and the C-lobe bound to H2 (Figure 7e), and the second is a 2:1 NHE1:CaM complex, with the CaM N- and C-lobes both interacting with H1 on two adjacent NHE1 C-tails, potentially stabilizing the dimeric state of NHE1 (Figure 7f).
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from NMR data and depicted in Figure 7f.

claims.claim: The total cellular [CaM] is 5–6 µM as measured in various cell types.
claims.source: Although the total cellular [CaM] is 5–6 µM as measured in various cell types, the global free Ca2+-CaM concentration in a cell has been estimated to be around 50 nM, that is, ~1% of the total [CaM] (Persechini and Stemmer, 2002; Saucerman and Bers, 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies measuring cellular CaM concentrations.

claims.claim: The global free Ca2+-CaM concentration in a cell has been estimated to be around 50 nM, that is, ~1% of the total [CaM].
claims.source: Although the total cellular [CaM] is 5–6 µM as measured in various cell types, the global free Ca2+-CaM concentration in a cell has been estimated to be around 50 nM, that is, ~1% of the total [CaM] (Persechini and Stemmer, 2002; Saucerman and Bers, 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies estimating free Ca2+-CaM concentrations.

claims.claim: CaM-mediated oligomerization has been reported for both soluble and membrane proteins.
claims.source: CaM-mediated oligomerization has been reported for both soluble and membrane proteins.
claims.evidence: Refers to established knowledge about CaM-mediated oligomerization.

claims.claim: Two ERα bind to one Ca2+-CaM, one in each lobe, to maximally activate transcription.
claims.source: Examples of the former include the ERα, with two ERα binding to one Ca2+-CaM, one in each lobe, to maximally activate transcription (Li et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies of ERα-CaM interaction.

claims.claim: The affinity of one CaM lobe for ERα is almost 100-fold lower than what we measured for H1 of NHE1.
claims.source: The affinity of one CaM lobe for ERα is almost 100-fold lower than what we measured for H1 of NHE1, further supporting a unique role of the 1:2 CaM:NHE1 complex.
claims.evidence: Comparison of measured affinities with literature values.

claims.claim: For SK channel monomers, 1:1 complexes with apo-CaM form through C-lobe binding, keeping the channel inactive; when [Ca2+]i increases, the N-lobe also associates with the channel, triggering dimerization and channel opening.
claims.source: Small-conductance Ca2+-activated K+-(SK) channel monomers form 1:1 complexes with apo-CaM through C-lobe binding, thereby keeping the channel inactive. When [Ca2+]i increases, the N-lobe also associates with the channel, triggering dimerization and channel opening (Barros et al., 2019; Lee and MacKinnon, 2018; Schumacher et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies of SK channel-CaM interaction.

claims.claim: For the eag1/Kv10.1 channel, the stoichiometry is 1:1, and it is proposed that CaM acts as a molecular clamp interacting with domains from neighboring subunits, thereby 'twisting' the pore closed.
claims.source: Another example is the eag1/Kv10.1 channel, which is inhibited by CaM. Also for this interaction, the stoichiometry is 1:1, and it is proposed that CaM acts as a molecular clamp interacting with domains from neighboring subunits, thereby 'twisting' the pore closed (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to study of eag1/Kv10.1 channel-CaM interaction.

claims.claim: CaM binding may contribute to NHE1 C-tail dimerization in a 2:1 (NHE1:CaM) stoichiometry.
claims.source: Based on our findings, it could be speculated that CaM binding contributes to NHE1 C-tail dimerization in a similar way as was observed for ERα, with CaM binding to H1 on two separate NHE1s in a 2:1 (NHE1:CaM) stoichiometry (Figure 7f), as shown in the ternary complex (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Speculation based on NMR structure data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 7f.

claims.claim: Ca2+-CaM could regulate NHE1 through electrostatic tuning of the NHE1:PI(4,5)P2 interaction.
claims.source: Finally, given the key role of anionic lipids including phosphatidyl-inositol(4,5)-diphosphate (PI[4,5]P2) in regulating NHE1 by interacting with the C-tail (Aharonovitz et al., 2000; Shimada-Shimizu et al., 2014), Ca2+-CaM could also regulate NHE1 through electrostatic tuning of the NHE1:PI(4,5)P2 interaction. Such mechanisms are reported for several other membrane proteins (Cao et al., 2013; Monteiro et al., 2014) and would be consistent with the folding of the NHE1-LID domain upon membrane interaction, bringing the CaM-binding region in close proximity to the NHE1-LID and the membrane (Hendus-Altenburger et al., 2020).

results.result: ITC experiments reveal that NHE1 peptides H1, H2, and H1H2 bind CaM with distinct stoichiometries and affinities. H1 binds CaM in a 1:2 (CaM:H1) stoichiometry with high affinity (Kd,1 = 27 ± 8 nM; Kd,2 = 42 ± 6 nM), H2 binds in a 1:1 stoichiometry with much weaker affinity (Kd = 9.0 ± 0.6 µM), and H1H2 displays two binding transitions with Kd,1 = 0.27 ± 0.07 nM and Kd,2 = 560 ± 15 nM.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 present ITC data with quantitative binding parameters, stoichiometries, and error estimates. The data are internally consistent, showing H1 has higher affinity than H2, and H1H2 exhibits biphasic binding. The measurements appear technically sound with appropriate replicates (n=3 stated in methods).

results.result: NMR titration experiments demonstrate that H1 binds to both CaM lobes with differential kinetics. At 1:1 CaM:H1 ratio, H1 preferentially binds the C-lobe, while at 1:2 ratio both lobes are occupied. Lineshape analysis yields koff,1 = 40 ± 5 s⁻¹ for C-lobe dissociation and koff,2 = 16 ± 3 s⁻¹ for N-lobe dissociation, indicating >10-fold faster association with the C-lobe.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C45 describe NMR titration data showing progressive binding of H1 to CaM lobes with quantitative kinetic parameters. The observations are consistent with the ITC stoichiometry data (C32-C33) and provide mechanistic detail. The lineshape analysis methodology is appropriate and yields reasonable rate constants.

results.result: NMR titration of H2 into CaM shows fast exchange kinetics with Kd = 16 ± 1 µM and koff = 2600 ± 100 s⁻¹. Chemical shift perturbations span both CaM lobes but are less pronounced for the C-lobe compared to H1 binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 present NMR data for H2:CaM interaction showing fast exchange and weaker binding than H1, consistent with ITC results (C34-C35). The Kd from NMR (16 µM) is somewhat higher than from ITC (9 µM), which the authors attribute to weak self-association of H2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), providing a reasonable explanation for the discrepancy.

results.result: The authors conclude that each CaM lobe can independently bind one H1 peptide with high affinity in a 1:2 complex (C-lobe slightly favored), while H2 binds CaM with lower affinity in a 1:1 complex involving both lobes.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are summary conclusions directly supported by the ITC (C32-C37) and NMR (C38-C48) data. The conclusions are consistent with all quantitative measurements and provide a coherent model of the binding interactions.

results.result: NMR analysis of CaM:H1H2 complexes reveals stoichiometry-dependent binding modes. At 1:2 (CaM:H1H2) ratio, each CaM lobe binds one H1 in a ternary complex with H2 uninvolved. At 1:1 ratio, the major state has N-lobe bound to H1 and C-lobe bound to H2, with a minor state showing opposite architecture. Signal broadening indicates dynamic equilibria between multiple states.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C59 describe complex NMR spectra of H1H2:CaM showing multiple binding modes. The interpretations are supported by spectral overlays with simpler H1 and H2 systems (Figures 3a-f). The detection of minor states and dynamic equilibria is consistent with the observed signal broadening. However, the complexity and exchange broadening limit structural precision.

results.result: SEC-MALS, DLS, and PFG-NMR confirm the stoichiometry and size of CaM:H1H2 complexes. SEC-MALS shows the 1:1 complex has a molecular weight of 25.0 ± 1.6 kDa (expected 25.5 kDa), and DLS/PFG-NMR show stepwise size increases from free CaM to 1:1 to 1:2 complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 present orthogonal biophysical data supporting the NMR-derived stoichiometries. The SEC-MALS molecular weight matches the expected 1:1 complex within error. The stepwise size increases by DLS and PFG-NMR are consistent with progressive complex formation. These data address concerns about higher-order oligomers.

results.result: The NMR solution structure of the 1:2 (CaM:H1) ternary complex shows both CaM lobes binding one H1 in their hydrophobic clefts. Individual lobes are well-defined (backbone RMSD: N-lobe = 0.77 ± 0.16 Å; C-lobe = 0.83 ± 0.18 Å), with flexible linker. Binding involves hydrophobic contacts (H1 residues L623, I631, I634, L635, N638, L639, T642, L646 with CaM methionines) and electrostatic complementarity (H1 positive residues with CaM negative surface).
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 describe the NMR structure with appropriate precision metrics (RMSD values, Table 4). The structure is consistent with the NMR data (C38-C45) showing 1:2 stoichiometry. The identification of specific interacting residues is supported by NOE data. The flexible linker is consistent with absence of inter-lobe NOEs. Structural statistics (Table 4) show good quality (95.7% residues in favored Ramachandran regions).

results.result: The NMR-derived C-lobe:H1 binding mode was present in the prior crystal structure (Köster et al., 2011) but manifested as crystal contacts between symmetry-related molecules rather than the intramolecular interaction observed in solution.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 reconciles the new NMR structure with the prior crystal structure by showing the C-lobe:H1 interaction exists in both but with different molecular contexts. This is supported by structural comparison (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and provides a reasonable explanation for the discrepancy between crystal and solution structures.

results.result: NMR experiments show that NHE1 H1H2 can bind apo-CaM (Ca²⁺-free) and that H1 binding stabilizes Ca²⁺ binding to the CaM C-lobe under Ca²⁺-limiting conditions (high EDTA), resulting in a state with Ca²⁺-loaded C-lobe and apo N-lobe.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 demonstrate Ca²⁺-dependent modulation of binding using NMR (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The observation that H1 increases C-lobe Ca²⁺ affinity is supported by spectral data showing C-lobe signals resembling Ca²⁺-bound state while N-lobe signals resemble apo state under Ca²⁺-limiting conditions. This reveals an avidity effect and expands the functional repertoire of the interaction.

results.result: PS120 cells stably expressing WT or variant NHE1 (H1-CR, S648A, S648D) show proper plasma membrane localization, comparable expression levels (variants slightly higher than WT), similar endogenous CaM levels, and similar steady-state pHi (~7.4-7.5). Basal acid recovery rates after NH₄Cl prepulse are not significantly different between cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 establish baseline cellular characterization. Immunofluorescence (Figure 5a) confirms membrane localization, western blots (Figure 5b-d) show expression levels, and pHi measurements (Figure 5e-g) demonstrate functional NHE1. The lack of basal differences is important for interpreting Ca²⁺-stimulated effects. Statistical analyses are appropriate (one-way ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis with exact p-values provided).

results.result: Ionomycin treatment significantly increases pHi recovery rate in WT NHE1-expressing cells compared to vehicle controls. However, H1-CR and S648D variants show significantly reduced Ca²⁺-induced NHE1 activation compared to WT, while S648A shows no significant difference.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 demonstrate functional consequences of mutations on Ca²⁺-dependent NHE1 activation using pHi recovery assays (Figure 5h-i). The data show clear statistical differences (p<0.05) between WT and H1-CR/S648D variants under ionomycin stimulation. The S648A result is interesting as it differs from S648D, suggesting phosphorylation-mimicking (not just absence) affects function. Appropriate controls and statistics are provided.

results.result: Proximity ligation assay (PLA) detects NHE1:CaM proximity (≤40 nm) in PS120 cells expressing WT NHE1. PLA signal does not increase with ionomycin treatment, and none of the three variants (H1-CR, S648A, S648D) abolish NHE1:CaM proximity despite their effects on Ca²⁺-induced activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 show that mutations affecting Ca²⁺-dependent function (C80) do not prevent NHE1:CaM proximity. PLA data (Figure 6a-b) are quantified appropriately (~400 cells per condition). The lack of ionomycin effect and persistence of proximity in variants suggests basal interaction is maintained. However, PLA detects proximity, not necessarily functional binding, which the authors acknowledge in Discussion (C108-C110).

results.result: In the NMR structure of the 1:2 (CaM:H1) complex, residues K641, R643, R645, and S648 are solvent-exposed when H1 is bound to either CaM lobe, and S648 does not form direct contacts with CaM.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 describe structural features relevant to understanding why mutations don't abolish proximity (C83). The NMR structure (Figure 6c-d) clearly shows these residues are solvent-exposed. This provides a structural rationale for why S648 phosphorylation might affect binding affinity (through electrostatic effects) without completely preventing interaction.

results.result: In vitro phosphorylation assays show Akt phosphorylates S648, while PKCδ phosphorylates T642, S648, and T653. ITC measurements demonstrate that S648 phosphorylation weakens H1H2:CaM binding ~10-fold (Kd,1 = 5 ± 4 nM, Kd,2 = 2700 ± 600 nM for pS648 vs. Kd,1 = 0.27 ± 0.07 nM, Kd,2 = 560 ± 15 nM for unphosphorylated).
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 demonstrate phosphorylation effects on binding. Mass spectrometry and NMR (Figure 6h, Figure 6—figure supplement 2) confirm phosphorylation sites. ITC data (Figure 6i, Table 1) show quantitative weakening of binding upon S648 phosphorylation. The ~10-fold effect on the second binding event is substantial and consistent with the functional effects (C80). The identification of additional PKC sites (T642, T653) is important for understanding regulation complexity.

results.result: Ionomycin treatment does not activate Akt in PS120 cells, and Akt inhibitor Akti-1/2 (which abolishes Akt activity) has no significant effect on ionomycin-stimulated NHE1 activity. Similarly, PKC inhibitors BIM I and Gö6983 do not significantly affect Ca²⁺-dependent NHE1 activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 show that despite S648 being phosphorylated by Akt and PKC in vitro (C86-C87), these kinases are not required for Ca²⁺-induced NHE1 activation under the conditions tested. Western blots (Figure 6g) confirm Akt inhibition, and pHi assays (Figure 6e-f) show no effect of kinase inhibitors. This suggests other kinases regulate S648 in this context, as the authors conclude (C111, C117).

results.result: The authors propose a model where NHE1:CaM complexes adopt multiple states depending on Ca²⁺ and protein concentrations: apo-CaM binding (Ca²⁺-free), partial Ca²⁺ loading (C-lobe Ca²⁺-bound, N-lobe apo), 1:1 complexes (N-lobe:H1, C-lobe:H2), and 2:1 complexes (both lobes binding H1 from different NHE1 molecules, potentially stabilizing NHE1 dimers).
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 synthesize the in vitro data (C32-C70) into a comprehensive model (Figure 7). The model is well-supported by the ITC stoichiometries, NMR binding modes, and Ca²⁺-dependence data. The 2:1 complex potentially stabilizing NHE1 dimers (C97) is speculative but reasonable given the NMR structure showing each lobe can bind H1. The model accounts for the observed complexity and provides testable predictions.

results.result: The authors conclude that NHE1:CaM interactions are highly dynamic, forming multiple complexes with different stoichiometries and structures in vitro, tunable by NHE1, CaM, Ca²⁺ concentrations and S648 phosphorylation. In cells, Ca²⁺-induced NHE1 activity is reduced by H1-CR and S648D mutations but not by Akt inhibition, while NHE1:CaM proximity persists. The NMR structure suggests CaM may stabilize NHE1 dimers, and multiple kinases likely regulate S648.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C119 are summary conclusions integrating all major findings. The in vitro structural diversity is well-established (C32-C70), the cellular functional effects are demonstrated (C79-C80), the disconnect between proximity and function is shown (C81-C83), and the kinase-independence is documented (C89-C92). The conclusions are appropriately cautious about the dimerization role ("may contribute") and acknowledge complexity. The work provides significant new insights into NHE1:CaM regulation.

results.result: Background claims establish that CaM is a ubiquitous Ca²⁺-binding protein with two lobes connected by a flexible linker, binding up to four Ca²⁺ ions and interacting with diverse targets including membrane proteins. CaM binding modes are diverse, though common features include α-helix propensity, positive charge, and hydrophobic residues.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 provide established background on CaM structure and function, supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These are standard knowledge claims that contextualize the study.

results.result: Background claims establish that NHE1 is a plasma membrane Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger functioning as a dimer, consisting of a 12-TM transport domain and a ~300-residue disordered C-terminal regulatory domain. NHE1 regulates pHi and multiple cellular functions, with hyperactivity implicated in cancers and cardiovascular disease. Activity is regulated by phosphorylation and binding partners including CaM.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C17 provide established background on NHE1 structure, function, and regulation, supported by appropriate citations. These contextualize the study's focus on NHE1:CaM interaction.

results.result: Background claims establish that CaM binds NHE1's cytoplasmic domain in a Ca²⁺-dependent manner, causing alkaline shift in pHi sensitivity and activation. Two CaM-binding sites (CB1 and CB2) bind with different affinities (Kd ~20 nM and ~350 nM). CB1 is essential for Ca²⁺ responsiveness. S648 phosphorylation has been reported to have both inhibitory and stimulatory effects on NHE1 in different cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C27 summarize prior work on NHE1:CaM interaction, appropriately citing original studies. The conflicting reports on S648 (C23) motivate the current study's investigation of this residue. The prior affinity measurements (C25-C26) provide context for the new ITC data.

results.result: Background claims describe the prior crystal structure of CaM:NHE1 showing an unusual extended configuration with H1 binding the C-lobe "back side" and H2 binding the N-lobe hydrophobic groove. SAXS analysis showed poor fit to the crystal structure, motivating re-evaluation of the complex in solution.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 describe prior structural work (Köster et al., 2011) that revealed an unusual binding mode and discrepancy between crystal and solution data. This directly motivates the current NMR study to characterize the solution structure.

results.result: Background claims establish that S648 is located at the C-terminal end of H1 and can be phosphorylated by Akt. Prior studies showed S648A mutation increased CaM binding in cardiomyocytes (with phosphorylation proposed to inhibit), while S648 phosphorylation was required for NHE1 activation in fibroblasts, indicating context-dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 summarize prior conflicting findings on S648 that motivate the current study's detailed investigation. The cell-type differences are appropriately noted and provide rationale for the experiments.

results.result: Discussion claims provide context that total cellular CaM is 5-6 µM but free Ca²⁺-CaM is ~50 nM (~1% of total). CaM-mediated oligomerization occurs for various proteins including ERα (2:1 binding with ~100-fold lower affinity than NHE1 H1), SK channels (apo-CaM binding C-lobe, Ca²⁺ triggering N-lobe binding and dimerization), and eag1/Kv10.1 (CaM as molecular clamp).
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C104 provide literature context for interpreting the results, with appropriate citations. The comparison of ERα affinity to NHE1 H1 (C102) uses the current study's data to highlight the uniqueness of the NHE1 interaction. These contextual claims support the Discussion's arguments.

results.result: Discussion speculates that CaM may contribute to NHE1 C-tail dimerization in a 2:1 stoichiometry (similar to ERα), which would explain prior reports of C-tail dimerization sites and kinetic evidence for dimerization in NHE1 regulation. Alternatively, Ca²⁺-CaM could regulate NHE1 through electrostatic tuning of NHE1:PI(4,5)P₂ interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 are speculative proposals about functional mechanisms. While the 2:1 complex structure (C62-C66) supports the possibility of CaM-mediated dimerization, direct evidence for this in cells is lacking. The PI(4,5)P₂ mechanism is also speculative, though supported by analogy to other systems (citations provided). These are reasonable hypotheses requiring future testing.

results.result: Discussion proposes explanations for why mutations affecting function don't abolish NHE1:CaM proximity: phosphorylation effects may not be strong enough to fully prevent interaction in vivo, cellular interactions may occur through other proteins (e.g., calcineurin) or lipids, and apo-CaM binding plus lack of ionomycin effect suggest NHE1:CaM complexes are present at all times.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 are speculative explanations for the PLA results (C81-C83). While the proposals are reasonable (supported by apo-CaM binding data C68 and prior work on NHE1 interactions), they remain untested hypotheses. The PLA method's limitations (detecting proximity, not functional binding) are appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Discussion concludes that S648 phosphorylation by both Akt and PKC in vitro, combined with lack of Akt/PKC inhibitor effects on Ca²⁺-stimulated activity, indicates multiple kinases can regulate S648. T653 has been implicated in regulation by Rho kinase and β-Raf.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 draw reasonable conclusions from the kinase data (C86-C92). The in vitro phosphorylation by multiple kinases combined with lack of specific inhibitor effects supports the conclusion that multiple kinases can act on S648. The T653 information (C112) from literature adds to the complexity. However, the specific kinase(s) responsible in the ionomycin context remain unidentified.

results.result: The authors speculate that similar regulatory mechanisms and structural diversity may be relevant for CaM interactions with many other membrane proteins.
results.evaluation: Claim C120 is a broad speculation about the generalizability of findings. While the diversity of CaM:NHE1 complexes is well-established, whether this level of complexity applies to other membrane proteins requires case-by-case investigation. The speculation is reasonable but untested.
